t: Count Different Palindromic Subsequences — Interval DP on a 4-Letter Alphabet
o: We must count distinct non-empty palindromic subsequences of s (only letters 'a'–'d'), modulo 1e9+7. Distinctness is by sequence content, not by position — e.g. in "bccb" the subsequence "bcb" occurs twice but counts once. This deduplication is the crux: naive enumeration is exponential, so we need DP over intervals where palindromes are classified by their outer character. In "bccb": single chars give b, c; pairs give bb, cc; length-3 gives bcb; length-4 gives bccb — total 6. With n ≤ 1000, an O(n^2) interval DP fits easily, and the tiny alphabet lets us handle duplicates by looking at the first/last occurrence of each letter inside an interval.
k: Any palindrome's content is determined by its outermost character pair plus the inner palindrome, so classify answers by the boundary character.
For interval [i,j], only the first and last occurrence of each letter c inside it can produce a maximal palindrome starting/ending with c — everything else is a duplicate.
The alphabet has size 4, so per interval we examine at most 4 letters, giving O(4·n^2) time.

a.i: Define dp(i, j) = number of distinct palindromic subsequences within s[i..j]. For each letter c present in s[i..j], let l be its first occurrence and r its last. If l == r, the palindrome c contributes 1. If l < r, then c...c wraps any palindrome from dp(l+1, r-1), contributing 2 + dp(l+1, r-1). Summing over the (at most 4) distinct letters never double-counts, because two different letters yield different contents, and for a fixed letter only the extreme occurrences generate new palindromes.
s: Memoize on (i, j); base case i > j gives 0.
For each letter c in 'a'..'d', find leftmost index l ≥ i and rightmost index r ≤ j with s[index] == c using precomputed next/prev tables or linear scans.
If no occurrence, skip. If l == r, add 1 (the single char).
If l < r, add 2 + dp(l+1, r-1): the char alone, doubled, and wrapped around every inner palindrome.
Return the sum modulo 1e9+7; answer is dp(0, n-1).
a.t: O(4·n^2) time — each of O(n^2) intervals scans up to n positions for up to 4 letters (or O(1) amortized with precomputed next/prev tables).
a.sp: O(n^2) for the memo table plus O(n) recursion stack.

a.i: Same recurrence as Approach 1 but computed iteratively over increasing interval lengths, avoiding recursion overhead. For each interval [i, j], we find the first and last occurrence of each letter by scanning inward from both ends simultaneously — since there are only 4 letters, at most 8 steps suffice to pin down all extremes. The counting rule is identical: each distinct letter contributes either 1 (single occurrence) or 2 + dp[l+1][r-1] (wrapping all inner palindromes).
s: Allocate dp[i][j] for all 0 ≤ i ≤ j < n; initialize dp[i][i] = 1.
Iterate interval length len from 2 to n, and start i from 0 with j = i + len - 1.
Scan k from i upward and from j downward collecting first/last positions of each of the 4 letters (stop early once all found).
For each letter with first occurrence l and last r: add 1 if l == r, else add 2 + dp[l+1][r-1].
a.t: O(4·n^2) time — for each of O(n^2) intervals, the two-pointer scan touches at most 8 characters per letter before finding extremes.

w: In an interview, lead with the top-down formulation since the recurrence is easier to explain, then mention it converts directly to bottom-up. Key pitfalls: forgetting that a single occurrence of a letter still yields one palindrome; double-counting when summing over letters (must use only extreme occurrences); off-by-one errors around empty inner ranges (dp of an empty interval is 0, so "cc" correctly adds 2). Edge cases: strings of length 1 (answer 1) and strings with one repeated letter like "aaaa" (answer 4: a, aa, aaa, aaaa). Follow-ups: generalize beyond 4 letters (then precompute next/prev occurrence tables to keep the scan O(alphabet)), or count palindromic substrings instead of subsequences (different problem, expand-around-center works).
